subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and cardiac tumors
vignette: A 34-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of recurrent nosebleeds. She has had several episodes of epistaxis per week since childhood. On examination, there are small red-purple lesions on her tongue and lips that blanch completely when pressed with a glass slide. Urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria. Her father had similar lifelong nosebleeds and died after a spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Buerger disease
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome)
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Takayasu arteritis

explanation_correct: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is an autosomal dominant disorder of blood vessels. Findings include blanching telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes (eg, tongue), recurrent epistaxis, arteriovenous malformations in the brain, lung, and liver, GI bleeding, and hematuria. The autosomal dominant family history, blanching tongue lesions, and hematuria are classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a defect in collagen causing hyperextensible skin, easy bruising, and joint hypermobility; it does not produce blanching mucosal telangiectasias with recurrent epistaxis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Buerger disease is an inflammatory, thrombosing vasculitis of distal extremities in heavy smokers, presenting with claudication and gangrene, not mucocutaneous telangiectasias.
explanation_incorrect.D: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis causes necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis with sinusitis, hemoptysis, and glomerulonephritis; c-ANCAs are positive and epistaxis is not due to telangiectasias.
explanation_incorrect.E: Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous disease of the aorta and its major branches, typically in young Asian women with diminished pulses, not inherited telangiectasias and hematuria.

educationalObjective: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu) is an autosomal dominant disorder with blanching mucocutaneous telangiectasias, recurrent epistaxis, AVMs, GI bleeding, and hematuria.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and cardiac tumors
vignette: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after the sudden onset of severe headache and vomiting followed by unresponsiveness. Noncontrast CT of the head shows an acute intracerebral hemorrhage in the right parietal lobe. MRI angiography demonstrates a high-flow vascular lesion with direct communication between an artery and a vein and no intervening capillary bed.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hemorrhage?

options.text: Rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm
Rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms
Hemorrhagic transformation of an ischemic stroke
Rupture of an arteriovenous malformation
Venous sinus thrombosis with venous infarction

explanation_correct: An arteriovenous malformation is an abnormal, high-flow connection between an artery and a vein without an intervening capillary bed, and it is the most common cause of intracranial hemorrhage in children. AVMs can occur as isolated lesions or as part of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, where they arise in the brain, lung, and liver and increase the risk of high-output cardiac failure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysms are associated with hypertension, polycystic kidney disease, and Ehlers-Danlos or Marfan syndromes, and typically produce subarachnoid hemorrhage in adults, not intraparenchymal hemorrhage in young children.
explanation_incorrect.B: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms occur in small penetrating vessels of patients with chronic hypertension and cause basal ganglia, thalamic, or pontine hemorrhages in older adults.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hemorrhagic transformation of an ischemic stroke occurs in adults with large infarcts or after reperfusion therapy, not as the de novo presentation of a high-flow vascular lesion in a child.
explanation_incorrect.E: Venous sinus thrombosis causes venous infarction and hemorrhage, classically in hypercoagulable states such as pregnancy or dehydration; it does not produce an artery-to-vein connection on angiography.

educationalObjective: Arteriovenous malformations (abnormal high-flow artery-vein connections) are the most common cause of intracranial hemorrhage in children and may occur in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and cardiac tumors
vignette: A 42-year-old woman presents after two episodes of syncope, each occurring when she sat up quickly. For the past 3 months she has had low-grade fevers and a 4-kg weight loss despite normal appetite. Cardiac auscultation reveals a low-pitched sound early in diastole after S2 at the apex. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a mobile mass in the left atrium attached near the interatrial septum.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's fever and weight loss?

options.text: Recurrent microembolization of tumor fragments causing fever
Production of interleukin-6 by the tumor
Production of tumor necrosis factor-alpha by infiltrating neutrophils
Secondary infective endocarditis on the surface of the mass
Paraneoplastic secretion of antidiuretic hormone

explanation_correct: This patient has a left atrial myxoma, the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults; 90% occur in the atria, mostly the left atrium. Myxomas can produce interleukin-6, which causes constitutional symptoms such as fever and weight loss. The mobile mass also acts as a ball-valve obstruction of the mitral orifice, explaining the positional syncope, and may auscultate as an early diastolic tumor plop that mimics mitral stenosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Myxomas can embolize fragments, but embolization causes stroke or peripheral ischemia rather than the chronic fever and weight loss described here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha is not the cytokine classically produced by cardiac myxomas; interleukin-6 production by the tumor accounts for the constitutional symptoms.
explanation_incorrect.D: Infective endocarditis of a myxoma is rare and would feature sustained bacteremia, murmurs changing from valvular destruction, and embolic infarcts, not a tumor plop with positional syncope.
explanation_incorrect.E: ADH secretion causes hyponatremia and water retention, a paraneoplastic pattern seen with small cell lung cancer, and does not explain fever and weight loss from a left atrial mass.

educationalObjective: Cardiac myxomas, the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults (90% atrial, mostly left atrium), produce IL-6 causing fever and weight loss and can cause ball-valve obstruction with syncope and an early diastolic tumor plop.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and cardiac tumors
vignette: A 9-year-old boy with a history of seizures and hypopigmented ash-leaf macules on his trunk undergoes echocardiography after a murmur is heard. The study shows multiple masses within the ventricular walls. A biopsy of one of the masses is performed.
question: Which of the following is the most likely histologic finding in the biopsied mass?

options.text: Gelatinous material with myxoma cells immersed in glycosaminoglycans
Malignant proliferation of immature striated muscle cells
Metastatic melanoma cells containing intracellular melanosomes
Dense proliferation of benign fibroblasts and collagen
Hamartomatous growths of striated muscle

explanation_correct: Rhabdomyomas are the most frequent primary cardiac tumors in children, are associated with tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf spots, seizures), are hamartomatous growths histologically, and are more common in the ventricles. The boy's tuberous sclerosis features and intraventricular masses point directly to rhabdomyoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Gelatinous myxoma cells immersed in glycosaminoglycans describe a cardiac myxoma, the most common primary tumor in adults, which arises in the atria rather than the ventricular walls of a child.
explanation_incorrect.B: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a rare malignant cardiac tumor of childhood; the masses here are benign hamartomas associated with tuberous sclerosis, not malignant proliferation of immature muscle.
explanation_incorrect.C: Metastatic melanoma is the most common cardiac tumor overall, but metastases occur in adults with known melanoma and are not hamartomatous ventricular masses in a child with ash-leaf spots.
explanation_incorrect.D: Proliferation of fibroblasts and collagen describes a cardiac fibroma, which is not the classic tumor associated with tuberous sclerosis.

educationalObjective: Rhabdomyoma, a hamartomatous ventricular tumor, is the most frequent primary cardiac tumor in children and is associated with tuberous sclerosis; myxoma (gelatinous myxoma cells in glycosaminoglycans) is the adult counterpart.
